description: How Bovell shapes the play around the seasons and gives each child their own central revelation.
content_html:
A Year in the Price Garden

Andrew Bovell's Things I Know to Be True is structured around the four seasons of a single year. Each season belongs primarily to one of the four adult Price children — Pip in spring, Mark in summer, Ben in autumn, Rosie in winter — and each season delivers a revelation that unsettles the suburban family. This seasonal frame is not decorative. It is the play's dramatic structure: four interlocking acts of unequal emotional weight, building cumulatively towards a shock at the play's close that retrospectively re-orders what the audience believed they understood.

The structure is broadly chronological, moving through a calendar year. Yet within each season, time is not always linear. Bovell inserts direct address monologue passages, particularly through the voice of Rosie, who acts as a narrator-figure. These moments allow characters to speak from a future perspective, as if looking back on what the season revealed, creating a layer of dramatic irony that gives the audience information slightly ahead of the other characters.

Key Fact

The four seasons map onto four children: spring (Pip), summer (Mark), autumn (Ben), winter (Rosie). Each season brings a revelation that tests the Price family's sense of who they are and what holds them together.

The Kitchen and the Garden as Twin Centres

The action takes place primarily in two spaces: the Price family kitchen and the suburban rose garden Bob tends throughout the year. The garden is both a literal and symbolic space. As a symbol, it holds Bob's emotional life: his sense of order, control and beauty in a world where his children's revelations keep threatening to undermine the certainties he has built. On stage, the garden can be established simply — a few rose bushes, a soil patch, a garden chair — and the blocking often places Bob alone there before another character arrives to disturb his peace.

The kitchen, meanwhile, is the domestic centre: Fran's territory, associated with food, practicality and direct speech. In production, the two spaces can coexist on stage simultaneously, so that a director's choice about proxemics between characters moving between kitchen and garden becomes itself a staging language. When a child crosses from the kitchen to join Bob in the garden, the move marks a shift in emotional register.

A common student error is to retell the four revelations as plot summary. Examiners reward analysis of why Bovell chose this structure. Consider what the seasonal frame achieves: each revelation lands at a different emotional temperature. Spring carries the energy of new beginnings; Pip's departure is therefore against the grain of hope. Autumn's association with decay and harvest perfectly frames Ben's arrest. Winter's coldness amplifies the shock of the play's ending.

The structural symmetry also allows Bovell to make each child's season resonate against the others. The audience accumulates information across the year, so by winter they carry the emotional weight of every previous season. As a designer, you might reflect this accumulation through a gradually changing lighting palette — brighter, warmer in spring, progressively more stripped and cool by winter — creating a visual arc that reinforces the structural one.

Frantic Assembly Movement Within the Seasonal Frame

The play was co-developed with Frantic Assembly, the British physical theatre company, and their influence shapes where moments of stylised movement are inserted into the seasonal structure. At emotional peaks — moments too large for naturalistic dialogue — the characters enter Frantic Assembly movement sequences: chair duets, contact lifts and round-by-through-under partner work. These sequences do not replace the dialogue; they abstracted the emotion that dialogue cannot fully express.

In structural terms, these movement passages function like the heightened soliloquies in classical drama: they signal that the play is stepping outside its naturalistic register to allow the audience to feel rather than analyse. As a performer, you must understand where you are in the seasonal structure when one of these sequences begins — the physical demands of a spring chair duet carry a different emotional charge from a winter one.

Key Fact

Frantic Assembly movement sequences interrupt the naturalistic dialogue at moments of heightened emotion. They are structural devices, not decoration: they show what characters feel but cannot say.

The Shock Ending: Dramatic Irony in Retrospect

Bovell builds a late-play revelation about Bob — a revelation that casts new light on everything that has preceded it. This is a structural device Bovell uses across his work: the thing you think you know is retrospectively undone. The audience carries their understanding of Bob through all four seasons and then, in winter, discovers they have been watching with incomplete information.

For a director, the challenge is to stage the ending so that the tableau at the play's close resonates with every earlier tableau the audience has seen. The ending must feel both surprising and, in retrospect, inevitable — the hallmark of precisely engineered dramatic structure. In production, designers often use a sudden, stark shift in the lighting state to mark the revelation: a wash that was warm and amber throughout the summer season becomes a cold, bare white or a near-blackout, so that the structural shock is felt as a physical change in the space.

Students sometimes treat the direct-address passages as straightforward narration — information delivery. In fact, they are structurally complex. Rosie's monologues are spoken from a temporal perspective that is partly ahead of where the action has reached. This means the audience is in a state of partial dramatic irony: they sense that things will go wrong before they go wrong. As a performer playing Rosie, the challenge is to hold both timeframes in your body: the innocence of the present tense and the knowledge of the future. Physically, this might mean a stillness that contrasts with the movement of the scenes around her, positioning her slightly apart — at upstage centre, separated from the family activity downstage — to suggest her dual temporal position.
exam_tip_html:
For the 12-mark question asking you to analyse playwright intentions, the most common error is describing what happens in each season rather than explaining why Bovell chose to structure the play this way. Ask yourself: what does the seasonal frame allow Bovell to do that a conventional act structure would not? How does the accumulation of revelations create a specific effect on the audience by the time the final shock lands? Your answer must refer to what the playwright wants the audience to think or feel at that moment — not just what the characters do.

For the 20-mark extended staging response, remember you must address both performer and designer choices. A strong answer for a plot-and-structure question might discuss: the lighting state transitions between seasons (designer), the use of upstage/downstage space for the garden and kitchen (director/set designer), and the vocal register a performer uses in a direct-address monologue compared to a naturalistic dialogue scene (performer). All three must be anchored to specific named moments in the play.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bovell structures the play around four seasons, each foregrounding one child's revelation, building cumulative emotional weight towards a late-play shock that re-orders what the audience believed.
  • The kitchen and the rose garden are twin centres: the garden is a recurring symbol of Bob's emotional life; proxemics between these spaces carries meaning for a director.
  • Frantic Assembly movement sequences are structural devices, not decoration: they mark the moments where naturalistic dialogue cannot hold the emotion, and a designer's lighting choices should reflect the seasonal arc throughout.

practice_questions.text: Name the playwright of Things I Know to Be True.
What is meant by the term 'dramatic structure'?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic correct answer (e.g. the way a play is organised or divided into sections); 1 mark for development linking structure to the creation of meaning or effect on the audience (e.g. the sequencing of scenes and revelations to build tension or surprise).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses the seasonal frame to give structural shape to the play's four revelations.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the seasonal structure and its mapping to four children (1); explanation of how one or more seasons carries a specific emotional charge that contrasts with or amplifies its revelation (1); reference to accumulation of revelations and audience effect (1); reference to a specific structural device such as direct address or the shock ending (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the effect of placing Bob's rose garden at the centre of the play's staging. How might a set designer communicate the garden's symbolic function?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the garden as a symbol of Bob's emotional life or sense of order; 1 mark for a specific design choice (e.g. a single rose bush as a focal point, or soil under Bob's feet contrasting with the kitchen's hard floor); 1 mark for explaining the effect of that choice on audience understanding of Bob's character; 1 mark for linking the garden's staging to a named moment or transition in the play.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Bovell uses dramatic structure to control the audience's understanding of Bob Price across the four seasons. Consider what is revealed, what is withheld, and what effect the late revelation has on the audience's experience of the earlier scenes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed analysis of Bovell's structural intentions, including the seasonal frame as a deliberate device, the function of Rosie's direct-address monologues in creating dramatic irony, the withholding of information about Bob, and the retrospective re-ordering the shock ending creates. The student explains the intended effect on the audience at specific structural moments with concrete reference to dramatic methods. No plot summary.

Secure: Identifies seasonal structure and the shock ending, explains that Bovell withholds information about Bob, and makes some reference to audience effect. One or two structural devices mentioned (e.g. direct address, seasonal arc). Mostly analytical rather than descriptive.

Developing: Describes what happens in the four seasons without sustained analysis of why Bovell structures the play this way. Some attempt to address audience effect but largely plot-driven.

Emerging: Retells the plot across the seasons with little or no analysis of playwright's intentions or structural choices.

practice_questions.text: As a director staging the moment when the final revelation about Bob is made in winter, explain how you would use lighting, set, proxemics and at least one performer choice to communicate the shock to the audience. Refer to specific choices and their intended effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full range of staging disciplines addressed. Lighting: specific state change named (e.g. a sudden shift from an amber wash to cold white or near-blackout, using a profile lantern to isolate Bob); set: a specific design choice for the garden in winter (e.g. bare rose stems, frost effect on the ground cloth); proxemics: specific positioning of characters at the moment of revelation, with justification; performer: specific vocal (e.g. a drop in volume, a pause before a line) and physical choice (e.g. stillness contrasting with movement elsewhere). Every choice anchored to the named moment with an explanation of the effect on the audience.

Secure: Most disciplines covered; at least one named lighting choice and one named performer choice; generally concrete but perhaps one area described generically (e.g. 'dark lighting' without naming lantern type or state change); audience effect mostly addressed.

Developing: Relevant staging ideas but generic language ('sad lighting', 'slow movement'); disciplines covered superficially; limited or no reference to the named moment; effect on audience implied rather than explained.

Emerging: List of ideas without justification or reference to specific staging choices; mostly descriptive; no reference to the named moment.

A speech in which a character speaks directly to the audience, stepping outside the scene.
The use of space and distance between performers to express relationship and status.

glossary_terms.definition: The way a playwright organises the action of a play, including act/scene divisions, framing devices and the sequencing of events.
A speech in which a character speaks directly to the audience, stepping outside the action of the scene.
The position and arrangement of performers relative to each other and to the audience, used to express status, relationship and emotional state.
An object, image or element of staging that carries significance beyond its literal function, representing an idea, relationship or emotional state.
The arrangement and movement of performers on stage throughout a performance.
A still image created by performers holding positions, used to encapsulate a moment of significance or to frame the end of a scene.
The quality, colour and intensity of light on stage at a given moment.
A Frantic Assembly movement technique in which two performers use chairs as props, creating lifts, slides and counter-balance sequences.
